title: The Oak and the Reed

full_text:
A massive, ancient oak tree stood upon the high bank of a winding river, towering proudly over the landscape with colossal limbs that had withstood centuries of sun and rain. At the water's edge below grew a slender, delicate green reed that swayed with every passing breeze.

The oak looked down with pitying contempt upon the fragile plant: "How unfortunate is your lot, little reed! A tiny sparrow alighting upon your stem bends you double, and the gentlest zephyr makes you bow your head in helpless submission. Look at me! My mighty trunk defies the thunderbolts, my roots grip the deep foundations of the earth, and I laugh at the fury of the storm!"

The slender reed bowed gently to a passing gust and replied softly: "Your sympathy is generous, mighty oak, but do not grieve for me. The winds do not harm me; I bend before their breath, and so I never break. It is you who should beware your rigid pride."

That night, a violent hurricane roared out of the northern sea. The tempest howled with demonic fury, lashing the valley with torrents of rain and furious gales that tore branches from the woods.

The slender reed bent flat against the water, yielding to the overwhelming blast without resisting its power.

The mighty oak stood rigid and defiant, battling the storm with all the stubborn strength of his ancient timber. But the gale blew with relentless, crushing fury. With a deafening CRACK that echoed across the valley like thunder, the colossal trunk snapped at its base, and the great giant was uprooted and cast lifeless into the surging river waters.

When the morning sun rose over the calm valley, the slender reed straightened itself in the warm light, while the shattered giant lay ruined in the mud.
moral: It is better to bend and adapt with the storm than to break through stubborn pride.
